Congratulations on making it to the end of the week. This is Jonathan Wosen, STAT’s West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter. We’ve got an eclectic lineup for you today, including a look at how declining vitamin K shots are impacting infants, why medical records often don’t tell the full story about women’s health, and results on health and science-related ballot measures across the country.

Oh, and a study that unearths evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb (pun intended). Let’s dig in.

That’s how much higher the risk of brain bleeding during the first six months of life was in infants who didn’t receive a vitamin K shot, compared to those who did. Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, which plays an essential role in forming blood clots. That’s why the American Academy of Pediatrics has for more than 60 years recommended that newborns get the one-time shot shortly after birth. But medical mistrust has led a growing number of parents to turn down the injection; the share of newborns who weren’t given vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025.

That trend has had grim consequences, according to a study published Thursday in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Researchers looked back on data from more than 5 million infants born between 2017 and 2025 and found that, compared to infants given vitamin K, those who weren’t given K had a 47% higher risk of bleeding during their first six months and a 169% higher risk of dying while bleeding shortly after birth.

In recent years, the Kratom plant and related synthetic products have become omnipresent across smoke shops and gas station shelves, buoyed by proponents who extol these products’ pain-relieving powers. But public health experts have raised serious concerns about the potential dangers of kratom — and the fact that these products are not closely regulated.

It’s a debate that is confusing to many; two-thirds of Americans have never even heard of kratom. STAT’s Theresa Gaffney has you covered with this timely explainer on the drug. The piece covers how a plant that has been chewed and brewed for centuries in Southeast Asia due to its stimulant-like effects has quickly risen in popularity in the U.S., where some users say kratom has eased chronic pain and helped them get off opioids.

Theresa also digs into 7-OH and MGPI, semi-synthetic related products that some experts worry are especially addictive. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say that they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular. But for now, data on overdoses and deaths are murky.

You might think that your medical records are an objective account of your health. But they’re not, write epidemiologist Annemarie Hirsch and sociologist Jennifer Silva. The pair recently published a study in which they paired electronic medical records and interviews with 87 women about pain, illness, and encounters with the health care system.

Many of the women described trust-breaking encounters with health care providers and misdiagnoses, but these moments were rarely documented. The authors point to the story of a woman who lived with debilitating pelvic pain for more than a decade as a poignant example. Doctors at first dismissed her pain as related to obesity, pivoting to mental health after she lost weight. Notably, the turning point only came after her husband joined her for an appointment, and she was ultimately diagnosed with endometriosis. Her medical records chronicle this diagnostic odyssey, but they don’t capture the frustration and disillusionment she experienced after years of having her pain downplayed. Hirsch and Silva write that such stories raise concerns about the use of AI to advance women’s health.

“These tools are only as good as the data in the medical record,” they write. “If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.”

Many Democrats are still celebrating the blue wave that handed their party control of both the House and Senate. But that momentum didn’t fully translate to health-related ballot initiatives across the country. As of late Thursday, voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington had approved or were on track to endorse measures that would prohibit transgender youth from participating on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Voters in four states with abortion-related ballot measures chose to preserve the status quo, with Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia choosing to maintain abortion rights while Idaho preserved the state’s existing ban.

Meanwhile, California voters appear on track to endorse Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research. The measure has sparked controversy because its main backer is also the co-founder of an institute poised to receive half the funds. South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned a state Medicaid expansion on federal financial support holding steady. And Massachusetts voters can breathe easier (well, sort of) after a measure to repeal the state’s recreational marijuana law was defeated handily.

You can read more from me and Theresa Gaffney. But first, let’s stick with weed for a moment longer.

Early writing by the ancient Greek historian Herodotus — known for his foundational text on the Greco-Persian wars and banger quotes like, “of all possessions a friend is the most precious” — is a key source used by historians to support the idea that prehistoric communities were smoking weed. Archaeological evidence is hard to come by (plants are perishable!) and just as tricky to interpret. But a new paper, published yesterday in Science, offers compelling evidence of ritual cannabis use in a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb.

The monumental burial mound included a log cabin-like structure, one coffin, and the remains of multiple individuals and horse sacrifices. There, archaeologists found hundreds of cannabis seeds, a handful of which were analyzed and dated to the first decade of the eighth century BCE. But there was an even rarer finding: two long braids of human hair containing significant amounts of the psychoactive compound cannabinol. “Although proving intent in a prehistoric context will remain impossible,” the authors wrote, “the evidence is strongly in favor of intentional consumption for the plant’s psychoactive properties.”

Admittedly, this is not our usual fare. But the study is a good reminder that drug use is not a modern issue, but rather a phenomenon that’s been with us for millenia. — Theresa Gaffney

#5734. Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age

Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

#5732. CMS proposes rollbacks of 'excessively burdensome' Conditions of Participation

CMS proposes rollbacks of 'excessively burdensome' Conditions of Participation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services plans to trim several “unnecessary” requirements for hospitals and other providers participating in Medicare, including emergency services readiness requirements and staff training for obstetrical services that had been brought during the tail end of the Biden administration.

The proposed rule’s Conditions of Participation (CoP) rollbacks, shared late Thursday (PDF), followed a “comprehensive review” CMS conducted to identify and eliminate “obsolete, outdated and excessively burdensome regulations.”

Removing these, the agency estimated, would save $320 million and free up 3.26 million hours of staff time for provider organizations.

Among the chief changes is a repeal of requirements finalized in the 2025 Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and ASC Payment Systems rule that tasked hospital and critical access hospital emergency departments to be “continually prepared” to provide emergency screening or stabilization regardless of whether they provide relevant specialty services, which were made effective in July 2025.

The 2025 rule paired those with baseline staffing and care delivery standards, annual staff training and maternal quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) requirements around obstetric care, which are currently set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. CMS also proposed eliminating those requirements this week.

CMS under the prior administration had said these requirements would improve safety, quality and the timeliness of care delivery for pregnant women.

On the other hand, CMS' new proposed rule looks to add a new obstetrics requirement for hospitals and critical access hospitals tied to the collection of birth tissue, “including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious or personal reasons,” per a fact sheet.

Other proposed changes to the CoPs include clarification revisions to policies regarding distance-related eligibility for critical access hospital designation and to implement an exemption from the distance eligibility requirements for some critical access hospitals.

Long-term care facilities would also see changes around COVID-19 vaccination education for staff and uptake for residents, as well as exemptions for existing facilities from newer room occupancy and bathroom facility standards. Among other changes are removals or slim downs of respiratory illness data reporting requirements for multiple types of provider facilities.

The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days. Among these, CMS said it is interested in hearing from stakeholders on additional requirements for participating providers, including flexibilities for physician supervision of certified registered nurse anesthetists, expanding the scope of practice of nurse practitioners and physician assistants in long-term care facilities, and reducing barriers for new transplant programs to achieve initial certification.

#5731. Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal

Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

For two decades, researchers debated whether adeno-associated viruses, the small viruses used to deliver new genes into thousands of patients, could in certain cases drive tumors. That debate is over.

A series of cases this year has presented powerful evidence that adeno-associated viruses, or AAVs, can cause cancer, forcing researchers and families to weigh the newly confirmed risk against the technology’s lifesaving potential — and hopefully determine how to design better therapies in the future.

“It will change the calculus for some patients,” said Sam Mackenzie, a neurologist at University of Rochester, speaking specifically about spinal muscular atrophy patients.

#5729. Lp(a)-Lowering Pelacarsen Shows Huge Disconnect With Cardiovascular Outcomes

— After disappointing Lp(a) HORIZON trial, eyes turn to next-gen siRNA therapies

Lowering lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), did not translate into better cardiovascular outcomes in a secondary prevention population, at least not with pelacarsen in the Lp(a) HORIZON trial.

Among people with elevated lipoprotein(a) and pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD), pelacarsen was no help for reducing the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), or urgent coronary revascularization over nearly 5 years (HR 1.02 compared with placebo, 95% CI 0.90-1.15), reported Steven Nissen, MD, of the Cleveland Clinic, at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

No matter how the investigators sliced and diced the data, it was the same story: analysis of people with especially high lipoprotein(a), 90 mg/dL or higher, also yielded no benefit (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.15); pelacarsen similarly showed no efficacy regarding a modified cardiovascular endpoint not counting revascularizations, another composite endpoint including coronary heart disease rather than cardiovascular deaths, and the individual outcomes of MI, stroke, urgent revascularization, and cardiovascular death.

Beyond these "completely neutral" results, "tolerability issues were certainly very prominent" with pelacarsen, Nissen added during an AHA press conference, citing rates of adverse events leading to drug discontinuation of 20.6% with pelacarsen versus 7.5% with placebo.

Nissen stressed that it may be the end of the road for pelacarsen, but not the lipoprotein(a) hypothesis.

"The Lp(a) HORIZON trial is not the end of the story. Ongoing trials are studying different populations, like primary prevention, aortic stenosis, and different therapies, and siRNA, several siRNAs. A single trial does not provide definitive evidence of a lack of benefit of lowering lipoprotein(a) as a strategy to reduce cardiovascular risk," he said.

Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic CVD and aortic stenosis. It is a highly atherogenic particle considered unmodifiable with diet or physical activity, unlike LDL cholesterol. Estimates suggest one in five people worldwide have high lipoprotein(a).

Pelacarsen was an antisense oligonucleotide made to degrade the hepatic mRNA coding for apolipoprotein(a), an intermediate to the production of lipoprotein(a).

In Lp(a) HORIZON, pelacarsen did drastically reduce lipoprotein(a) and LDL cholesterol by an estimated 77.7% and 13.3%, respectively, relative to placebo. This was on top of existing secondary prevention therapies that had gotten baseline LDL cholesterol to a median 64.6 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure to 125 mmHg on average.

"Was there no room left for improvement? To the credit of the investigators, what was done was actually optimization of what we know to do already: optimize the LDL, optimize the blood pressure. If we do that, was there just no room left in these patients to further reduce the risk?" posed panelist Donald Lloyd-Jones, MD, ScM, of Boston University.

"Like Dr. Nissen, I personally would not recommend that we abandon considering Lp(a) as a potential causal risk factor or as a therapeutic target until we have a lot more data available in different patient populations, certainly in younger individuals and primary prevention populations, over longer periods of time and with ... different chemical strategies to try to inhibit this molecule," said Lloyd-Jones, a past president of the AHA.

Nissen noted that the siRNA therapies in development are potentially more tolerable and more effective while requiring less frequent administration. Already advancing to large-scale cardiovascular outcome trials, for example, are lepodisiran and olpasiran, with others further back in the pipeline.

There's also evidence that the now-familiar PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies reduce Lp(a) along with LDL cholesterol, which may partly explain some of their benefit in CVD risk reduction, according to Lloyd-Jones.

"We don't fully understand the biology here, and I think we need to continue to take a deeper dive into that biology so that we fully understand what it is about Lp(a) that serves as a marker of risk and potentially as a better target for our future therapies," he said.

"I really think you cannot close the door with a single negative trial," Nissen emphasized. "It's going to be my mission to try to convince the people that pay the bills, which is industry sponsors, not to pull the plug on trials because we really need to understand more."

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was a phase III cardiovascular outcomes trial conducted in nearly 800 sites in 42 countries. Eligible participants had a cardiovascular event 3 months to 10 years prior to enrollment and lipoprotein(a) levels 70 mg/dL or greater. They underwent a risk factor optimization period to ensure use of secondary prevention therapies.

Nissen's group had 8,350 individuals randomized 1:1 to pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo self-administered once monthly subcutaneously.

Mean age was just under 60, with about 27% of participants being women and 78% white. Median lipoprotein(a) was 236 nmol/L and hsCRP 0.8 mg/L. Nearly 80% of the cohort were on high-intensity statins.

Follow-up reached a median 57 months in the trial.

Nissen reported that his group sought to conduct additional exploratory analyses on account of the "unexpected" results of Lp(a) HORIZON.

In this extension report, there was still no argument to be made for pelacarsen's efficacy even after accounting for treatment adherence, first and repeated adverse events, and magnitude of 3-month lipoprotein(a) reductions, among other analyses.

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine and its extension report separately released in NEJM Evidence.

#5728. Industry Voices—New majority, new targets: Where healthcare fraud enforcement goes next

Industry Voices—New majority, new targets: Where healthcare fraud enforcement goes next" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Control of Congress has changed. The bipartisan appetite for scrutinizing practices across the healthcare industry has not. A new Democratic majority will arrive with no shortage of investigative priorities and only so much time to pursue them, but recent history suggests that healthcare is likely to be among them.

Affordability dominated this election cycle, and healthcare sits at the center of that debate. Combating fraud in Medicare and Medicaid has endured as a rare point of consensus precisely because it allows policymakers of both parties to say they are protecting patients and taxpayers at once. The open question is not whether that work continues, but where it is directed.

Congressional oversight largely reflects the priorities of the majority, which controls committee agendas, hearings and subpoenas. If recent history is a guide, a Democratic majority will gravitate toward a familiar set of concerns: the practices of large insurers including those involved in Medicare Advantage, the stewardship of hospital systems, the role of private equity, vertical integration across the industry, drug pricing, and the hyper-growth sectors attracting new investment.

The administration has elevated healthcare fraud to the top of its enforcement agenda. The Justice Department’s 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown charged 455 defendants in schemes involving more than $6.5 billion in alleged losses, with particular emphasis on Medicaid, while CMS suspended or revoked the billing privileges of more than 2,400 providers. In an October 1 directive, DOJ’s newly created National Fraud Enforcement Division went further, designating healthcare fraud its foremost corporate enforcement priority.

That model has been defined largely by scale: the number of defendants charged and the dollar value of alleged fraud identified. It will persist regardless of which party holds Congress, carried forward by entrepreneurial prosecutors and agents. What a Democratic majority could add is a complementary lens, one that weighs not only how much fraud is charged but how the industry’s largest and fastest-growing participants are organized, owned and paid.

The best predictor of the next two years may be the last several. While Democrats controlled the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, its October 2024 majority staff report examined post-acute care denials by the largest Medicare Advantage insurers. That inquiry did not end with the change in Senate control. In July 2026, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) sought updated data from one of those insurers on its prior authorization practices and its use of algorithms in coverage decisions. In the House, Democrats have called for closer scrutiny of insurer practices at nursing homes serving Medicare Advantage members.

Hospitals have drawn bipartisan attention as well. A January 2025 Senate Budget Committee report on private equity ownership of hospitals, led by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) and Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), raised concerns about staffing, hospital closures and distributions to investors. Months earlier, the Senate HELP Committee, then chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), subpoenaed the chief executive of a bankrupt, private equity-backed hospital system, and the full Senate voted unanimously to hold him in contempt after he declined to testify.

Concern extends to the structure of the industry itself. In May 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and Sen. Josh Hawley, joined by House members from both parties, reintroduced legislation that would require companies that own pharmacy benefit managers to divest their pharmacies, a measure that would force significant restructuring at some of the largest vertically integrated healthcare companies. Drug pricing has drawn similar scrutiny. In September 2024, the HELP Committee called the chief executive of a leading manufacturer of GLP-1 drugs to testify about U.S. prices for its diabetes and weight-loss treatments.

To the extent healthcare commands the new majority’s attention, the tools at its disposal are considerable. Committee chairs can compel documents and testimony by subpoena, require executives to testify under oath and publish staff reports that place internal records in the public domain.

Committees’ influence extends well beyond the hearing room. They can call on the Government Accountability Office and the HHS Office of Inspector General to examine particular programs, press CMS for data and refer matters to the Justice Department. Through legislation and appropriations, they can push for reforms in areas such as prior authorization, Medicare Advantage payment and transparency in private equity ownership. Oversight does not generate cases on its own, but it shapes where agencies look, which documents surface, and what insiders conclude is worth reporting. It shapes public opinion as well. Under the glare of hearings and headlines, a misstep that might once have been resolved quietly can escalate into a reputational and regulatory crisis.

Scrutiny of private equity tends to follow the sectors where investment has moved fastest. Applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy for children with autism illustrates the dynamic. The underlying demand is genuine: the CDC estimates that one in 31 children has autism spectrum disorder. Private equity firms have acquired more than 500 autism therapy centers over the past decade, and CMS reported in August that Medicaid and CHIP spending on ABA rose 421% between 2021 and 2025, far outpacing the 67% growth in the number of children served.

Whatever the causes of that gap, regulators have begun to respond. CMS issued a toolkit to help states strengthen oversight of ABA services, New York halved Medicaid reimbursement for certain ABA services in October, citing program integrity concerns, and Indiana paused new ABA provider enrollment. Sectors that combine rapid growth, substantial public funding and concentrated investor ownership are natural subjects of congressional interest, whichever party is in the majority.

Should the emphasis shift, Medicare Advantage is the likeliest starting point, given the sustained attention already paid to prior authorization, post-acute care denials, algorithm-driven coverage decisions and risk adjustment. Beyond it, the record points to three broader fronts that track how the industry is organized, owned, and paid. The first is integration, as lawmakers ask whether combining insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, pharmacies and providers under one corporate roof serves patients. The second is ownership, as committees examine how private equity affects staffing, billing and quality at hospitals and in hyper-growth sectors in healthcare. The third is pricing, particularly for prescription drugs.

For companies in these areas, the practical consequence is that exposure can arrive before any agency acts, and congressional and Justice Department scrutiny tend to reinforce each other. A single congressional letter can place internal records and decision-making in public view, and the attention that follows tends to encourage potential whistleblowers to come forward. Those insiders have strong incentives to take their concerns to the Justice Department as well. Under the False Claims Act, a whistleblower who files a qui tam suit may receive between 15% and 30% of the government’s recovery, and DOJ’s Corporate Whistleblower Awards Pilot Program offers awards for original information about criminal healthcare fraud, including fraud against private insurers.

The overlap in subject matter is considerable. The joint DOJ-HHS False Claims Act Working Group has named Medicare Advantage and drug pricing among its enforcement priorities, the same areas that have drawn sustained congressional interest. Testimony and documents made public through oversight can become a road map for relators’ counsel and prosecutors alike, and many healthcare fraud cases still originate with an insider.

For companies and investors, the prudent response does not depend on who holds the gavel. It begins with a clear-eyed understanding of where the business’s risks reside, followed by rigorous testing of controls in the areas of fastest growth and highest reimbursement, and a willingness to address problems early, with the benefit of counsel where the facts are uncertain. Enforcement priorities shift with each election. The expectation that companies will identify and remedy their own problems does not.

Kevin Lowell is a member at Miller & Chevalier and previously served as deputy chief of the National Fraud Enforcement Division at the U.S. Department of Justice.

#5727. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5725. Mayo Clinic Platform launches AI-driven clinical decision support tool

Mayo Clinic Platform launches AI-driven clinical decision support tool" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Mayo Clinic launched an AI-enabled clinical decision support solution embedded directly in electronic health record workflows. The CDS solution will put Mayo’s clinical knowledge and evidence-informed guidance at the point of care, rather than requiring clinicians to search across separate resources.

Mayo Clinic Platform, a strategic initiative from the Rochester, Minn.-based health system, developed the tool, and it will be expanded and updated over time, executives said. The solution draws on multiple clinical tools, reducing the need for clinicians to navigate independent resources to find trusted clinical information.

Mayo Clinic is making the CDS tool available to Mayo Clinic clinicians as well as healthcare organizations participating in Mayo Clinic Platform's provider programs. Mayo Clinic is essentially turning its clinical expertise into scalable AI infrastructure available beyond its own health system.

Beginning in November, eligible clinicians will have access to two key capabilities: a specialty-specific chat that covers more than 35 specialties and 22 clinical calculators available via chat or voice dictation.

Powered by a large language model, the specialty-specific AI chat tool surfaces relevant information to help clinicians reason through complex cases and cites responses from peer-reviewed literature. The tool is updated daily, giving clinicians access to relevant emerging evidence alongside established medical knowledge, executives said. The tool helps clinicians quickly answer patient-specific clinical questions, explore differential diagnoses and evaluate care options. And the specialty-specific AI chat mirrors Mayo Clinic's subspecialty model of care.

The clinical calculators, spanning cardiology, oncology, hepatology, endocrinology and other specialty use cases, provide industry-standard medical information and evidence-based decision support on clinical questions and patient care context. Proprietary Mayo Clinic-developed calculators are included in this tool, according to the health system.

"Clinicians have access to a vast amount of medical knowledge, but finding relevant information for individualized patient care takes valuable time," said Maneesh Goyal, Mayo Clinic Platform chief operating officer, in a statement. "With this new solution, we are bringing trusted Mayo Clinic knowledge directly into the clinical workflow so clinicians can spend less time searching for information across multiple resources and more time focused on patient care."

The platform is "designed to evolve" as new tools are added to Mayo Clinic Platform, executives say.

David C. and Flora C. Pratt Distinguished Chief Medical Officer for Mayo Clinic Platform Gelareh Zadeh, M.D., Ph.D., said in a statement the solution "does not replace clinical judgment."

"Mayo Clinic physicians have provided feedback on the different tools to ensure the solution supports clinicians and reflects Mayo Clinic's approach to patient care," Zadeh said.

#5724. The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis

Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

#5722. A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength

A simple daily fiber supplement may offer a surprising new way to relieve knee arthritis pain while improving muscle strength. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) who took a prebiotic fiber called inulin experienced significant reductions in pain, improved grip strength, and decreased sensitivity to pain.

The supplement also appeared to be considerably easier for participants to stick with than a digital physical therapy program. Only 3.6% of those assigned to inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21% of those assigned to physical therapy alone.

Published in the journal Nutrients, the findings suggest that improving gut health could become an additional strategy for managing arthritis. They also reveal an intriguing connection between the bacteria living in our digestive system, the way our bodies process pain, and muscle function.

A Simple Dietary Change Could Help Relieve Arthritis Pain

Knee osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is a major cause of chronic pain and disability, especially among older adults. The condition develops as the tissues within the knee joint, including the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorate. This can lead to pain, stiffness, swelling, and difficulty with everyday activities such as walking or climbing stairs.

Treatment typically focuses on reducing symptoms and maintaining mobility. Pain medications can provide relief but may cause unwanted side effects, while physical therapy and regular exercise can help improve joint function. However, keeping up with an exercise program can be difficult, particularly for people already struggling with persistent pain.

The new research raises the possibility that a simple dietary supplement could provide another way to manage symptoms.

"This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change -- adding a fiber supplement to your breakfast or yogurt -- could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function," said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, lead author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham.

The supplement tested in the study was inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods such as chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, and certain other vegetables. Unlike many nutrients, inulin is not broken down by digestive enzymes in the small intestine. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where beneficial bacteria can use it as food.

How Gut Bacteria May Influence Arthritis Pain

Researchers are increasingly discovering that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influences much more than digestion. These microbes interact with the immune system, produce biologically active compounds, and may even affect how the nervous system responds to pain.

Inulin is classified as a prebiotic because it nourishes certain beneficial gut bacteria rather than directly supplying living microorganisms, as probiotics do.

When bacteria ferment inulin, they produce substances known as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). One of the most important is butyrate, a compound that helps support the intestinal lining and can influence inflammation and biological pathways involved in pain.

The researchers found that participants taking inulin had increased levels of butyrate, suggesting that the supplement was influencing activity within the gut microbiome.

They also observed higher levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite and has also been linked to pain regulation and muscle health.

GLP-1 has attracted widespread attention because it is the hormone targeted by medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. However, the inulin supplement used in this trial was not a GLP-1 medication. Instead, researchers examined whether supporting beneficial gut bacteria could influence the body's own production of the hormone.

One particularly interesting finding was that higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength. Although this does not establish that GLP-1 caused the improvement, it suggests that changes originating in the digestive system may be connected to muscle function as well as pain.

To investigate these effects, the researchers conducted the INSPIRE trial, a six-week randomized controlled study involving 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis.

Participants were assigned to one of four treatment groups: a daily inulin supplement alone, digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and physical therapy, or a placebo.

This design allowed researchers to examine the effects of the supplement and exercise separately, as well as investigate whether combining them offered additional benefits.

Both inulin and physical therapy independently reduced knee pain, indicating that each approach provided meaningful symptom relief.

However, the supplement produced additional improvements that were not observed with physical therapy alone. Participants taking inulin demonstrated better grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity.

Pain sensitivity reflects how strongly the nervous system responds to potentially painful stimulation. Reducing that sensitivity could be particularly valuable for people with osteoarthritis, because persistent pain is not always explained by the amount of visible damage within a joint. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can also contribute to discomfort.

The improved grip strength was another unexpected result, suggesting that the supplement's effects might extend beyond the knee itself.

The researchers also found a substantial difference in how many participants completed their assigned treatments. Only 3.6% of the inulin-only group dropped out, compared with 21% of the physical therapy-only group.

This difference suggests that taking a daily fiber supplement may be easier to incorporate into a regular routine than following a structured exercise program.

A Surprising Connection Between Gut Health, Muscles, and Pain

Dr. Kouraki said: "Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective -- people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives."

Beyond the reduction in arthritis pain, the researchers are particularly interested in what the findings reveal about interactions between the digestive system, muscles, and nervous system.

The association between GLP-1 and grip strength raises the possibility of a broader biological relationship connecting gut health with physical performance and resilience as people age.

Senior author Professor Ana Valdes from the School of Medicine added: "The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation. This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly."

The findings are promising, but the trial was relatively small and lasted only six weeks. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be needed to establish whether the benefits persist, identify which patients are most likely to respond, and clarify the biological mechanisms responsible.

The results also do not suggest that fiber supplements should replace exercise or other established arthritis treatments. Instead, they point toward a potentially useful additional approach that could complement existing care.

The potential importance of this research becomes clearer when considering how many people live with persistent arthritis pain.

Professor Lucy Donaldson, Director of Research at Arthritis UK, said: "The pain of arthritis can severely impact quality of life. Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis.

"Researchers are starting to explore the role of the gut microbiome in our experience of pain. This exciting preliminary research highlights how diet and physiotherapy can act in different ways to have benefits for people with arthritis. We know a variety and balance of healthy foods, including fiber, and regular physical activity matter, and we're glad to be supporting research that explores how they work to help people with arthritis."

For people living with knee osteoarthritis, the findings offer an encouraging possibility: a relatively simple change in daily nutrition may help reduce pain while supporting other aspects of physical health.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the research suggests that treating arthritis may involve looking beyond the joints themselves. By exploring how gut bacteria influence inflammation, pain perception, and muscle function, scientists may uncover new ways to manage a condition that affects millions of people every day.

#5721. Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more

Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare mergers and acquisitions are in no short supply as providers, health tech companies, payers and other industry players look to expand their businesses and gain a competitive edge. Here’s a roundup of new deals that were revealed, closed, rumored or called off during the month of October.

Rush University System for Health and Endeavor Health announced plans to merge, becoming a 12-hospital nonprofit with nearly $11 billion in annual revenue. The resulting entity would command over 400 care sites, employ more than 46,000 people including over 3,400 clinicians, and reach over 2 million Northern Illinois and Northwest Indiana patients per year. The pair are targeting an early 2027 close and outlined plans to commit $1 billion of Endeavor funds toward care in the region.

Private equity firm CD&R and healthcare conglomerate McKesson plan to acquire Option Care Health, a provider of infusion therapy services, in a deal valued at $5.8 billion. The purchase gives equity holders a per-share offer of $32.05 and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. CD&R would be the majority stakeholder in the company, which is the country’s largest independent at-home and alternate site infusion services provider.

Bon Secours Mercy Health announced plans to acquire a majority stake in Surgery Partners, among the country’s largest outpatient surgical care companies, in a take-private deal valuing the acquiree at $5.7 billion. Bain Capital Private Equity will roll over its 39% share of the company as it's purchased by a Bon Secours affiliate at $23.50 per share. Surgery Partners includes more than 200 locations and about 5,000 affiliated physicians across 30 states. The organizations are targeting an early 2027 close.

Risant Health, Kaiser Permanente’s subsidiary value-based care platform, announced Integris Health as its next regional health system acquisition. Financial terms were not disclosed, though the deal aims for an early 2027 close. Integris is Oklahoma’s largest nonprofit provider with 10 acute and 10 specialty hospitals with $3.3 billion in total operating revenues during the 2025 fiscal year.

MultiCare Health System picked up the final needed regulatory approval to absorb Samaritan Health Services during October. The nonprofits then consummated their 18-hospital combination on Nov. 1.

Hackensack Meridian Health has signed a definitive agreement to pick up Central New Jersey’s Hunterdon Health, which would grow the state’s largest health system to 19 total hospitals. The agreement outlines a $200 million capital investment from Hackensack Meridian, plus another $30 million to roll out Epic’s electronic health record.

Cencora (formerly AmerisourceBergen) signed a definitive agreement to acquire American Oncology Network, a collection of more than 350 oncology providers, in a deal valuing the network at $2.4 billion. Cencora said it expects to pay $1.7 billion to increase its 4% interest to 75%.

Parkview Health is acquiring Ovation Healthcare, a nationwide shared services vendor for providers. The 16-hospital Indiana nonprofit did not disclose financial terms, but said it hopes to close the deal within weeks. Parkview views the pickup as an opportunity to boost its administrative capabilities, which could be offered to other rural systems.

Parkview Health also wrapped its acquisition of Goshen Health, a 105-bed hospital with a network of physicians.

Independence Health System, a five-hospital nonprofit in western Pennsylvania, joined the West Virginia University Health System on Oct. 1. The deal was announced late last year and brings a five-year, $800 million capital commitment from WVU Health System toward the Independence hospitals and communities, which will "immediately" begin operating under the WVU Medicine brand.

Kettering Health plans to add Knox Community Hospital as its 15th medical center. The Ohio systems signed a definitive agreement for their deal, which will include undisclosed commitments toward Knox’s facilities, equipment and technology.

Nationwide Children’s Hospital plans to acquire the pediatric practice of Knox Community Hospital in spring 2027. Nationwide plans to combine the practice with one of its affiliates and continue providing services to Knox.

Allegiance Health Management said it plans to divest four Louisiana hospitals: Minden Medical Center, Northern Louisiana Medical Center, Acadian Medical Center and Mercy Regional Medical Center. No potential buyers or deal timelines were given.

Orlando Health closed its acquisition of RMC Health System, an Alabama organization with a 375-bed medical center. The deal was first announced in April, and brings five years of “significant” investment into RMC’s facilities, equipment and technology.

HCA Healthcare sold 31 home health and hospital agencies to Deaconess Associations. The facilities were located across eight states. Financial terms were not disclosed.

MaineHealth added York Hospital to its Southern region, marking the 79-bed facility as the system’s tenth hospital.

Ascension Seton said it is acquiring three locations in the greater Austin area from Family Health Systems, one of which is the Auton-based Family Hospital. The deal is set to close later this year.

Cone Health entered an agreement to acquire three pharmacies in Reidsville, North Carolina: Carolina Apothecary, Belmont Pharmacy and Rx Care.

Humana struck a deal shifting out Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe for BlackRock for equity in a joint venture running about 150 of its CenterWell locations. The deal sees BlackRock buying out WCAS’ equity for about $2.8 billion.

Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey is acquiring the New Jersey operations of Summit Health, which includes CityMD urgent care sites. Financial details or a potential timeline were not disclosed.

Redesign Health plans to merge with Sheba Medical Center’s innovation arm, ARC Global, creating a roughly $2 billion company. The pair hope to build an end-to-end platform that helps health systems to turn ideas originating with their own clinicians and operators into technology products and standalone companies that can then be scaled across a global network. To help do so, the pair also agreed to acquire strategic advisory and intelligence firm AVIA.

Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, which provides hybrid clinical services and specialized care support for rural and regional health systems, the public virtual care company announced alongside its Q3 earnings. Financial terms were not disclosed. Teladoc leadership said picking up its longtime partner will help it grow with providers serving rural communities.

RadNet, an imaging center operator and seller of radiology technology, is acquiring Onrad, a teleradiology services company with 130 contracted radiologists. The deal is expected to close early next year and will bring Onrad shareholders a collective $350 million plus 5 million RadNet shares, with additional performance-based earnouts.

iRhythm wrapped its acquisition of cardiac remote patient monitoring company VitalConnect for $237.5 million. The deal will help iRhythm evolve from ambulatory cardiac monitoring toward “a broader cardiac monitoring and intelligence platform,” its CEO and president told Fierce Healthcare.

Zocdoc acquired insurance technology company Sohar Health, the first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history and part of its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Carenet Health, which provides patient engagement and navigation tools to over 400 healthcare partners, acquired Orbita, an AI engagement and communication company that does business with providers. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Tegria, a healthcare consultancy and services company, acquired cybersecurity, cloud hosting and managed IT services company CloudWave for an undisclosed sum.

Chapter, a Medicare navigation and retirement advisory company, has acquired Hively, a personalized retirement navigation and membership startup, for an undisclosed sum. The pair intend to launch in-person and online community programming for retirees surrounding retirement and aging topics, a move beyond Medicare navigation alone.

Sagility, a provider and payer technology services company, acquired Chirok Health, which offers clinical documentation improvement, medical coding and revenue integrity services for an undisclosed sum.

Investment firm Sopris Capital said it acquired Blackford Analysis, an AI medical imaging platform, from Bayer for an undisclosed sum. Sopris said it intends to deploy the company’s tools across its healthcare portfolio.

Emergence, a private equity firm, acquired digital intake and online reputation management software company Clinect for an undisclosed sum.

#5720. Avoiding Chemo in Breast Cancer; Psychedelic Medication for Depression

— Also in TTHealthWatch: treatment of Achilles tendinitis

TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

This week's topics include treatment of Achilles tendinitis, avoiding chemo in some types of breast cancer, imaging and cardiac stent placement, and a psychedelic medication in depression.

Well, a lot of people now are getting the coronary CT. It can provide a non-invasive assessment of the coronary artery disease. Since that's done before the procedure, can we use that information to guide therapy? Will it be as useful as using intravascular ultrasound?

Half of them were randomized to just using that information to guide stenting. And the other half, in addition, had intravascular ultrasound. And they assessed at 12 months what the rate of target vessel failure was. Those in the CTA [CT angiography] group, about 4.1% had target vessel failure. In the intravascular ultrasound, about 4.6%. Elizabeth: And a lot easier to do, sounds like, in providing this information a priori versus having it concomitant with the procedure.

In this case, they looked at this in participants who were 18 to 75 years of age with moderate to severe major depressive disorder that had been nonresponsive to previous attempts, two to five of them, to treat it with current antidepressant medicines. They were looking at two different dosages of this medicine, as I mentioned, administered intranasally, 8 mg and 12 mg. And their comparator was a 0.3 mg administration alongside with psychological support.

Their primary endpoint was a total score change in the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale from baseline to day 29. And then they had a number of secondary endpoints. They also note that their discharge readiness in comparison with other psychedelic medications, like psilocybin for example, was assessed starting 90 minutes after their dosing.

Basically, what they found, it was a little bit curious. This medicine did seem to have an impact. They called it durable. Their day 29 response rates were 35%, 34%, and 12% with regard to 8 mg, 12 mg, and the comparator 0.3 mg dose. Their remission rates were 26%, 18%, and 8% in that same dosing regimen. It's a little curious, isn't it? Because the 12 [mg] appears to have not quite as good results as the 8 mg dose. They also did note that there were adverse events, but these were more or less the same among all of the doses. The editorialist opines that in comparison to what we already know about things like ketamine and psilocybin, maybe this is something that might add to the armamentarium.

Rick: These individuals, to test the effect of the drug, had to be off their antidepressants. These are people that already have refractory depression. They take them off their antidepressants and they only treat them with this, and then they follow them over the course of 60 days. With the other drugs, it's 4 to 12 hours to have to be sitting around waiting. With this particular medication, most people go home in 2 hours. With regard to durability, it lasted for at least 60 days, a single dose. Pretty darn good.

Will it last longer than 60 days? What is the best dose strategy? What if you combine it with other antidepressants? And the last thing I would want to say, Elizabeth, is the people that were excluded from this study were people that have suicidal ideation because there's concern that the psychedelic drugs in individuals with depression and suicidal ideation may actually make those worse.

Elizabeth: The editorialist, of course, also points out the suicidality as an issue, as an exclusion criterion in this trial. So those people clearly need to be examined and studied carefully. Although exercise treatment is oftentimes recommended, about half the individuals do not get better and almost half these people end up getting additional treatments such as injections. They're putting 50 mL of saline between the Achilles tendon and what's called Kager's fat pad.

These injections sometimes have just saline, sometimes they have steroids, and sometimes they have a local anesthetic. And the thought is that there's a mechanical or ischemic disruption of the pain signaling and the steroid has anti-inflammatory effects. Is it really effective? Nobody has ever tested that before.

So 192 adults with Achilles tendinopathy received a sham small-dose injection, the high-volume injection with steroids, or a high-volume injection without steroids. And then they followed them about a year. There were no clear differences between the sham and the high-volume injections, either with or without steroids. It looked like there was an initial improvement in the people that got injections with steroids, but then there was a rapid decline.

However, when they looked at cost-effectiveness, it looked like the high-dose injection with corticosteroids was cost-effective. I kind of scratched my head and said, gosh, if there's no difference, how could that be more cost-effective? Well, during that initial 12 weeks where it looked like it was a little bit better, that's when people were able to return to work earlier. Even though at the end there was no difference, the fact that they were able to return to work a little bit earlier made it a little bit more cost-effective.

Elizabeth: Sounding like it's back to the drawing board for folks with this condition. I'm wondering, does it talk about the natural history of it? How long does it take to resolve in most people in the absence of treatment?

Rick: Really interesting, because they follow these individuals over the course of about a year. Most of the improvement occurred, even in those that had sham, somewhere between 3 and 6 months. It's a long time. The primary treatment is exercise and anti-inflammatory medications. Those take 3 to 6 months to work, so people have to be patient.

Elizabeth: Let's turn to Nature Medicine and let's look at this idea that, gosh, there are some women who might be able to forego chemotherapy in their HER2-positive early breast cancer. This is a trial that's been ongoing for a while and this is looking at the 5-year outcomes. The study initiated as a noncomparative phase II trial evaluating PET-guided pathological complete response [pCR]-adapted adaptation strategy to omit chemotherapy in women with HER2-positive early breast cancer. I say early, that was stages I through IIIA, and the breast cancer was operable. They were randomized to receive chemotherapy plus trastuzumab [Herceptin] and pertuzumab [Perjeta], or some of them actually ended up getting early chemotherapy, but just a couple rounds of it, and then endocrine therapy.

In the second group, their treatment was adapted according to their FDG-PET response after 2 cycles of chemotherapy and pCR. They previously reported that this de-escalation revealed a 3-year invasive disease-free survival of 94.3%. Here, they're looking at 5-year results using circulating tumor DNA findings.

After their median follow-up of 5.6 years, that number was almost 90%, 89.5% in that group who were randomized to have their circulating tumor DNA assessed along with the FDG-PET results. They only showed in that group one distant recurrence. What they're suggesting is that this might be a really important strategy for being able to look at women who might be able to forego that chemotherapy.

Rick: Standard therapy is you give chemotherapy with [a taxane and a platinum], and you also combine these HER2 antibodies, the two that you mentioned. OK. Maybe we can forego the chemotherapy if, in fact, people would just respond to the HER2 antibodies. That's what they showed. And about a third of those patients did respond just to the antibodies and it saved them the toxic side effects of chemotherapy. This is pretty amazing. Anytime we can minimize the toxicity, get a terrific result, that's great news.

Elizabeth: They do note that this notion of circulating tumor DNA at baseline or during treatment, when they were able to find out, was associated with inferior disease-free survival. What this suggests to me is that looking for the tumor's DNA in the blood has to really be employed as a clinical marker for both "this might be a strategy that's going to work for you" as well as "what's going on on an ongoing basis."

Rick: Yeah. And so, Elizabeth, you're right. They use two different techniques. One is imaging. The other used serum biomarkers. If your imaging looked like the tumor had resolved and there were no biomarkers, those were the best outcomes.

Elizabeth: I'm going to go out on a limb here and prognosticate that at some point, I think, that circulating tumor DNA will supplant imaging because, as we're well aware, frequently imaging misses a lot of metastasis in particular that can be in certain spots in the body where it's difficult to discern.

Rick: And I would suggest that both will be helpful.

Elizabeth: I think both for a while, and I'm guessing it will supplant. We'll see what happens.

On that note then, that's a look at this week's medical headlines from Texas Tech. I'm Elizabeth Tracey.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange. Y'all listen up and make healthy choices.
