#5596. ‘The American Dream Has an Address’—and Both Parties Are on Notice, Strategists Say

Democrats' historic midterm sweep will hand them control of Congress, but keeping it could depend on whether they can make housing more affordable, according to leading strategists from both parties.

"The American dream has an address," veteran Democratic strategist Donna Brazile told a room of real estate professionals in New Orleans on Saturday.

Speaking alongside conservative political strategist Shermichael Singleton at the National Association of Realtors®' NAR NXT conference, Brazile cautioned that Democrats' electoral victories were not an unconditional endorsement of their policies, but a demand for relief from the rising cost of living.

Singleton agreed, arguing that Republicans had already learned that lesson the hard way.

"Our voters felt we fundamentally failed," he said, pointing to rising fuel and food costs as well as younger Americans' inability to afford homes as examples of the administration's unfulfilled affordability promises.

Brazile warned that Democrats could face the same reckoning in 2028 if they fail to act.

"If you're not going to help build more houses and take care of the affairs of the American people, they will kick our [expletive] in two years," she said.

The affordability crisis that helped propel Democrats to victory Tuesday had been a liability for their own party just two years earlier—a fact that Brazile said is a warning to both parties heading into 2028.

"Affordability has been on the minds of American people now for two consecutive years," Brazile said, acknowledging that Joe Biden and Kamala Harris had failed to recognize the depth of voters' frustration ahead of the 2024 election.

And today, housing offers perhaps the clearest illustration of why that frustration has persisted.

Mortgage rates climbed from roughly 3% in 2021 to nearly 8% by late 2023, compounding a pandemic-era surge in home prices, Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, explained during a separate presentation Saturday.

And while borrowing costs have since eased, home prices continue to climb. Prices rose in approximately 78% of U.S. metropolitan markets during the third quarter of 2026, according to NAR's latest quarterly report.

Existing homeowners have benefited from that appreciation, with Yun estimating that the typical owner has gained nearly $200,000 in housing wealth since before the pandemic. Prospective buyers, meanwhile, face a considerably higher cost of entry.

The consequences are particularly stark for younger Americans. First-time buyers now account for just 22% of home purchases, while their median age has reached 40, matching last year's record high, according to NAR's newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers.

"Maybe the election result was partly reflecting that fact," Yun said, pointing to younger Americans struggling to enter the housing market.

For Singleton, 36, the frustration is personal.

"You do everything right. You get the college degree. You get the graduate degree. You start the family. You can't afford anything," he said.

Singleton purchased his first home at 28, but said many of his friends, now approaching or entering their 40s, still can’t afford to buy.

And with millennials and Gen Z now accounting for a substantial share of the electorate, Singleton argued that housing access could become a more decisive factor in how younger Americans vote.

Amid deep political divisions, Brazile and Singleton's agreement on the urgency of the housing crisis was striking. And already, there's a powerful precedent for cooperation on the issue.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, enacted in July, received overwhelming support from both parties, passing the Senate 85-5 and the House 358-32. The legislation aims to boost supply by reducing regulatory barriers, expanding financing opportunities, and supporting new approaches to construction.

But passage was only the first step. Many provisions still require implementation or funding, and their effects on the market could take years to materialize.

Singleton sees opportunities to build on that foundation by addressing barriers closer to home, including local permitting delays, construction costs, and tariffs on Canadian lumber.

"One of the things that I hear about often from them is that the length of time it takes to get something approved is very costly," he said, referring to conversations with builders.

He also proposed investing in training younger Americans as electricians, plumbers, and other skilled tradespeople to help build the millions of homes the country needs.

It's an idea echoed by Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Association of Builders, who identified workforce development as a bipartisan priority in an exclusive interview with Realtor.com following Democrats' sweep of the state's elected offices.

"The more folks we can get in the business, that'll drive down those labor costs," Norman said.

Brazile, meanwhile, said Democrats' affordability agenda places housing alongside groceries, energy, and family expenses, with an emphasis on cutting red tape and expanding supply.

"Affordability, affordability, affordability. It's not a slogan that Democrats can use again unless they do something about it," she said.

But delivering on those promises will require something neither party has consistently demonstrated in recent years: a willingness to compromise.

"We have the money, but we need the will," Brazile said.

In an emotional moment of the one-hour session, Brazile recalled working with Republican President George W. Bush to secure federal assistance after Hurricane Katrina devastated the city in 2005.

Despite their political differences, Brazile said she worked with the administration to secure funding for housing recovery, infrastructure, and a new veterans' medical center.

"That's bipartisanship. That's compromise. That's what it looks like," she said.

Her closing message to the real estate agents in attendance was to bring that same commitment to the newly elected lawmakers who will shape housing policy.

"You know the stories because you live it every day," she told them, urging agents to share the experiences of families struggling to afford homes.

And with a new Congress preparing to take office, Brazile argued, that firsthand knowledge could help turn promises of affordability into policies that deliver.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5594. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5593. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5589. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.

#5588. HelloNation Examines Common Dental Problems in Children With Pediatric Dental Care Insights From Dr. Andrew Beuttenmuller

The article outlines prevention strategies for cavities, gum irritation, and early alignment concerns in children.

WATERTOWN, N.Y., Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What are the most common dental problems in children, and how can you prevent them? A HelloNation article provides clear answers, featuring insights from pediatric dental care professional Dr. Andrew Beuttenmuller of Watertown Pediatric Dentistry.

The HelloNation article explains that common dental problems in children include cavities, gum irritation, and early tooth alignment concerns. These issues often appear as children's teeth grow and develop, but consistent care and early attention can often address or prevent them. The article highlights that understanding these patterns is essential for effectively managing kids' dental problems in Watertown, NY; families can follow along at home with professional guidance.

Cavities in children remain a major concern. The article notes that tooth decay develops when sugars interact with mouth bacteria, creating acids that weaken enamel. Young children are especially at risk due to developing hygiene habits and frequent exposure to sugary snacks and drinks. The article emphasizes that preventing cavities in kids starts with daily routines and less sugar.

The article also discusses gum irritation kids experience, often called gingivitis, as another early concern. This condition can appear as redness, swelling, or bleeding gums, typically caused by plaque buildup along the gumline. The article describes how consistent brushing and flossing play a key role in preventing this issue and supporting overall pediatric dental care.

The article also addresses early concerns about tooth alignment, including crowding, spacing, and bite issues. While some changes are part of normal development, the article explains that early monitoring can help identify when intervention may be beneficial. Pediatric dental care providers can track these developments and guide families on the next steps when needed.

Prevention is a central focus throughout the article. It explains that proper twice-daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste is a foundational habit for preventing dental problems in kids. Families in Watertown, NY, can implement. Supervision during brushing helps ensure children clean thoroughly, while flossing removes plaque between teeth where brushes cannot reach. These habits directly support efforts to prevent cavities in kids and reduce gum irritation.

Diet is another important factor the article discusses. Limiting sugary snacks and drinks reduces the risk of cavities in children, while encouraging water supports oral health. The article notes that balanced meals with fruits, vegetables, and calcium-rich foods help strengthen teeth and gums. These dietary habits support long-term pediatric dental care and reduce the risk of common dental problems in children.

Routine dental visits are also emphasized as a key part of prevention. The article explains that regular checkups allow dental professionals to identify early signs of cavities in children, gum irritation that kids may not notice, and early tooth alignment concerns. Professional cleanings and fluoride treatments further support strong enamel and ongoing oral health.

The article concludes by noting that building positive habits early can have lasting benefits. When families focus on kids' dental problems, children in Watertown, NY can develop strong routines that continue into adulthood. Addressing common dental problems in children early helps support both oral health and overall confidence.

#5587. Mynd.ai Announces Change to American Depositary Share Ratio

ALPHARETTA, Ga., Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mynd.ai, Inc. (NYSE: MYND) ("Mynd" or the "Company"), a global provider of interactive technology and AI solutions for education and commercial customers, today announced that it will change the ratio of its American Depositary Shares ("ADSs") to its ordinary shares from one ADS representing ten (10) ordinary shares to a new ratio of one ADS representing seventy-five (75) ordinary shares. For the Company's ADS holders, the change in the ADS ratio will have the same effect as a one-for-7.5 reverse ADS split.

The ADS ratio change is expected to become effective on or about December 7, 2027 (U.S. Eastern Time), subject to completion of the applicable procedures with the Company's depositary, Citibank, N.A. (the "Depositary"), and other relevant parties. The ADSs will continue to trade on the NYSE American under the symbol "MYND," with a new CUSIP number of 628988206.

Following the effectiveness of the change, each ADS will represent seventy-five (75) ordinary shares of the Company, compared with ten (10) ordinary shares previously. The ordinary shares of the Company will not be affected by the change in the ADS ratio, and no ordinary shares will be issued or cancelled in connection with it.

The exchange of every seven and one-half (7.5) then-held ADSs for one new ADS is expected to occur automatically on the effective date, with the then-held ADSs being cancelled and new ADSs issued by the Depositary. Fractional new ADSs will not be issued in connection with the change in the ADS ratio. Instead, fractional entitlements to new ADSs will be aggregated and sold by the Depositary, and the net cash proceeds from the sale, after deduction of applicable fees, taxes and expenses, will be distributed to the applicable ADS holders in accordance with the terms of the deposit agreement.

ADS holders are not required to take any action. ADSs held in brokerage accounts will be adjusted automatically, and holders of certificated ADSs will receive instructions from the Depositary. The Company will pay the Depositary's fees and charges in connection with the surrender, cancellation, exchange, and issuance of ADSs effected as part of the ADS ratio change. #5585. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5583. AGNT says housing market is tough but not broken, points to ‘unmatched’ agent value

On AGNT’s Q3 2026 call, CEO Leo Pareja said the housing market remains difficult but is resetting to normal. AGNT reported revenue up 6% to $1.4 billion, a $4.3 million net loss, and 131,546 sides, up 8%.  AI Summary

Executives at AGNT, the parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome, two RealTrends Verified firms, are not beating around the bush when it comes to their thoughts regarding the current state of the U.S. housing market.

“To be direct, [the market] remains challenging, and we’re planning accordingly,” Leo Pareja, AGNT’s newly appointed CEO, said on the firm’s third quarter 2026 earnings call with investors and analysts Thursday evening.

Pareja said that while company executives expect the market to stay “difficult” for a while, they do not feel that the market is “broken.”

“It’s a market that’s resetting to normal after two record booms or warped expectations. Life events still force people to move, and in a market that requires real skill, the agents who are doing the work are taking the share,” said Pareja, a 2026 HousingWire Vanguard. “That’s where we’re well positioned. We have scale. We have a value stack for agents that we believe is unmatched. We have a competitive compensation structure and a strong agent base that’s increasingly productive, and we’re up for the challenge.”

As it looks to tackle this challenge, Pareja said the firm is focusing on four key targets for the rest of the year: agents, innovation, operating efficiency and margin expansion.

When it comes to agents, executives said this is where the acquisition of real estate franchisor NextHome comes in, as it has allowed the company to create a multimodal platform. “Independent agents, team leaders and franchise owners can all find a home built for the way they want to grow,” Pareja said.

In addition, executives also highlighted the tools and technology AGNT provides agents and brokers with to run their businesses.

“The goal is simple: help agents sell and manage their business, get paid smoothly, and provide better training and support at every step,” Pareja said. “Our intention is to earn the right to continue to be the most agent-centric brokerage on the planet.”

As for innovation, company executives highlighted their recent launches of MCP First AI of Choice and AGNT OS.

“Our stock ticker AGNT represents where the company is going. It’s a full modernization of how eXp runs, agent first from the ground up, built for a world you’re actually operating in today. MCP is the front door; AGNT OS is the whole house. It’s the full modernization of how we run. From how agents get paid to how a transaction moves to how they’re supported from day one,” Pareja said.

Finally, when it comes to margin expansion, executives highlighted some of their ancillary services efforts, including LUXVT, Revenos and the recently announced Revenos Mortgage joint venture with Newrez. Additionally, Pareja said that in the future, the company believes the NextHome franchise system will be a contributor to overall gross margin.

An improved gross margin is something the firm is looking for after it recorded a net loss of $4.3 million in Q3 2026, compared to net income of $3.5 million a year ago. This loss came despite a 6% year-over-year increase in revenue to $1.4 billion. Of note, however, is a 7% annual increase in operating expenses to $87.9 million.

While the financial results may not have been as strong as the company would have hoped for, the firm did see an 8% annual increase in transaction side count to 131,546 transactions, totaling $59.3 billion in sales volume, which was up 10% from a year ago.

In addition to this, the company closed Q3 with 87,457 agents and brokers on its platform, up 5% year over year, with 44% of the new additions joining teams. Executives noted that over 90% of the firm’s agent attrition came from the “less productive cohort” of agents, with nearly 50% of the nonproductive agents to leave the firm in the U.S. also leaving the industry.

AGNT also addressed the recent announcement of Open Real Estate, a national residential real estate data-sharing initiative, which it helped found alongside  HomeServices of America, Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group, all RealTrends Verified firms.

“The idea is simple. A brokerage or an agent would create a listing once using a minimum set of standard fields, and it would be shared with participating members and distributed to local MLSs, home search sites, and other platforms,” Pareja said.

“When listings are fragmented or kept out of view, buyers can miss homes and sellers can reach fewer potential buyers. Open Real Estate is designed to work alongside MLSs to combat market fragmentation, and it’s open to every brokerage in America as a free participating member.”

Pareja clarified that while AGNT is one of the four founding equity members, Open Real Estate is not a consolidating subsidiary of AGNT; it’s a standalone company that will have its own board of managers and leadership, which will be assembled in the coming months.

“AGNT shares Open Real Estate’s conviction that access, information and transparency should be a benefit, not a barrier, to both buyers and sellers,” Pareja said.

So far, Pareja said the startup costs for Open Real Estate experienced by AGNT have been “very modest and not material.”

“Going forward, costs will be borne by all the founding members, not just AGNT alone. As the venture builds out key leadership and moves ahead with platform development, we expect costs to increase over the next two quarters,” Pareja said. “We don’t expect that increase to be material to AGNT’s results.”

#5582. Accrete Signs Data Agreement with TenderAlpha to Deepen Supply Chain Risk Insight for Federal Customers

NEW YORK, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Accrete, the cognitive infrastructure company building Knowledge Engines for autonomous work, today announced that it has signed an agreement with TenderAlpha, a global provider of government contracting and supply chain data. The agreement brings TenderAlpha data into Accrete's Argus for Supply Chain Influence, giving defense and civilian agency customers greater visibility into the companies, suppliers and component parts behind the products and systems they rely on.

Across the government, supply chain visibility has become a priority. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) requires closer scrutiny of defense suppliers, and civilian agencies face growing pressure to understand risk in critical food, agricultural and medical product supply chains. Agencies need a clearer view of the sub-tier relationships and sources where risk often goes unseen.

"Supply chain risk isn't a data aggregation problem. It's a judgment and tacit knowledge problem," said Prashant Bhuyan, Founder and CEO of Accrete. "Human expertise doesn't scale fast enough to get ahead of foreign influence threats, and burying analysts under mountains of disconnected data only makes it worse. Accrete's Knowledge Engine captures and scales the tacit knowledge of individual analysts and the organization itself. It grounds reasoning models in that judgment so they become trusted agents. With TenderAlpha's data in Argus, those agents can do in minutes what would ordinarily take teams of exceptional analysts months or years."

"Our customers need to understand supply chain risk faster and at a deeper level than ever before," said Bill Wall, CEO of Accrete AI Government. "Adding TenderAlpha data gives us greater insight into the obscured vulnerabilities and threats inherent in complex global supply chains. It gives defense and civilian agency teams a robust picture of who is really behind the products and components they depend on, so they can act before a vulnerability becomes a problem."

By combining TenderAlpha data with Argus for Supply Chain Influence, powered by the Accrete Knowledge Engine and its supply chain expert agent, Accrete customers will be able to:

"Exposing complex supply chain risk requires connecting the dots across disparate layers that are very rarely combined," said Martin Tsanov, CEO and co-founder of TenderAlpha. "The fusion of TenderAlpha's global B2B relationship and trade data with government contracting and subcontracting data within Argus' cutting-edge multi-tier graph architecture equips national security agencies with the comprehensiveness and visibility needed to proactively identify hidden dependencies and secure critical supply chains."

The TenderAlpha agreement is part of Accrete's ongoing investment in the data and analytics that federal customers need to protect the Defense Industrial Base and the critical supply chains Americans depend on. Customers using Argus for Supply Chain Influence will gain access to these expanded insights in early 2027.

Accrete builds cognitive infrastructure for government and enterprise customers. Founded in 2017, Accrete's Knowledge Engine platform unifies fragmented systems, siloed data, tacit knowledge, and decision-making into a continuously learning universal system of intelligence. Knowledge Engines give agents the shared context to reason, collaborate, decide, and act across the full complexity of an organization. As AI makes intelligence abundant, judgment is the scarce resource, and Accrete's Knowledge Engines encode the expert judgment organizations accumulate over decades so agents can be trusted with consequential decisions. Accrete's customers span Fortune 500 enterprises as well as U.S. defense and national security agencies. From commercial operations to national security missions, Accrete's platform enables expert agents that deliver superintelligence designed for high-stakes environments. Accrete AI Government LLC, based in Alexandria, VA, is the federal subsidiary of New York-based Accrete, Inc.

Founded in 2014, TenderAlpha delivers high-quality, structured data products designed to support investment analysis, risk assessment, and market intelligence. TenderAlpha serves financial institutions, asset managers, and risk-rating and research professionals, offering deep insights into global G2B and B2B transactional trends. For more information, visit www.tenderalpha.com.

#5581. NRMLA asks Congress to restore HUD housing counseling funds

NRMLA asked congressional appropriators to restore rescinded HUD housing counseling funds tied to the HECM process. The group said mandatory third-party counseling is required to legally close federally insured reverse mortgages.  AI Summary

The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) is urging Congress to restore funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)’s housing counseling program, warning that cuts could disrupt the origination of federally insured reverse mortgages.

In a Nov. 2 letter to congressional appropriations leaders, NRMLA President Steve Irwin raised concerns about the presidential pocket rescission of appropriated funds for HUD’s housing counseling program, specifically the funding that supports the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) program.

NRMLA said independent, third-party counseling is a statutory requirement for every prospective HECM borrower. Under Section 255 of the National Housing Act, borrowers must receive counseling from a HUD-approved agency before a loan can close.

A counseling certificate issued by a certified counselor is required for a HECM loan to be legally closed, the trade group said.

The association also emphasized that lenders cannot pay for a borrower’s counseling session, direct borrowers to a particular counseling agency or use an agency affiliated with the lender. These restrictions are intended to ensure seniors receive objective information about reverse mortgage costs, obligations and alternatives.

Because lenders are prohibited from funding or steering the counseling process, NRMLA said federal appropriations are essential to maintaining the independent counseling infrastructure required for HECM originations.

Without the funding, the association warned, mandatory counseling could become less accessible and affordable for seniors, potentially creating obstacles to loan closings and limiting access to the federally insured reverse mortgage program.

The HECM program allows eligible older homeowners to access their home equity to support aging in place and improve their financial security. Irwin asked congressional leaders to take action to restore the funds, arguing that the funding is necessary to preserve the program as a housing finance option for seniors.

“We respectfully urge you to take the necessary action to restore the appropriated HUD housing counseling funds so that eligible seniors may continue to benefit from the HECM program,” he wrote.

The association represents more than 300 member companies and more than 2,000 member delegates. Its members originate more than 90% of reverse mortgages, according to the letter.

#5580. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

#5579. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5577. Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B

Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a deal valued at $5.3 billion.

The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.

Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.

The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.

Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.

Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.

According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team.

Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.

The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.

Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.

Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.

#5576. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5575. Blend posts smaller Q3 loss, warns of steeper mortgage revenue drop ahead

Blend Labs reported Q3 revenue of $32.9 million, up 1% year over year, and cut its GAAP operating loss to $2.6 million from $5.3 million. Mortgage suite revenue slipped 2% as funded loans on the platform fell 4% to 194,000 and value per loan reached $81.   AI Summary

Blend Labs narrowed its loss in the third quarter and logged its strongest period of sales in more than three years, even as rising mortgage rates pressured loan volumes and its core mortgage suite revenue declined.

Total revenue in the third quarter was $32.9 million, up 1% from the same period in 2025, the company reported Thursday. GAAP operating loss was $2.6 million, an improvement from a $5.3 million loss a year earlier.

“The market got harder, but we’re moving faster than ever,” Nima Ghamsari, co-founder and head of Blend, told analysts on an earnings call. “When we spoke in August, mortgage rates were about 6.8%. After the Fed raised rates in September, they hit a high of north of 7.5%. And as you can expect, applications dropped with them — purchase and refinance both.”

Blend closed 26 new deals and expansions during the quarter. In dollar terms, the company said, these moves represented more than twice the combined value of its first- and second-quarter deals.

Churn notices in the quarter represented about $2 million of annual revenue, an improvement from roughly $3 million in the second quarter. Based on a lighter churn environment in the first quarter and subsequent improvement, Blend said year-to-date gross revenue retention is in the mid-90% range.

“Three takeaways for today: One, We had our best sales quarter in more than three years; two, Autopilot went from six customers to 10 and the pipeline behind it is now big enough to size and growing; three, next year the market may not help us. Converting Autopilot pipeline is how we’re going to grow,” Ghamsari said.

Revenue from Blend’s mortgage suite totaled $17.4 million in the third quarter, down 2% year over year. The platform handled 194,000 funded mortgages, a 4% decline from the same period last year, and economic value per funded loan was $81.

In a compressed market, lenders are relying on Blend’s Rapid Mortgage and Rapid Home Equity solutions to lower per-loan costs and accelerate consumer-facing processes “when every basis point counts,” Ghamsari said.

For the fourth quarter, Blend guided total revenue to a range of $27.7 million to $29.7 million, a decline of about 8% to 15% year over year. Mortgage suite revenue is expected to fall 23% to 28% from the prior-year period, reflecting lower industry volumes and mix shifts.

Executives said potential fourth-quarter deals could contribute about $5 million in incremental revenue in 2027 as implementations go live. “Next year the market may not help us,” Ghamsari said.

Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote that Blend is “executing on what it can control against a weak mortgage market” and that “early traction with budding AI products (Autopilot) is encouraging.”

“We continue to think upside in the shares will be capped until there is visibility into a more meaningful and sustained acceleration in revenue growth (thus driving more scaled profitability), which the weak mortgage backdrop pushes out,” the analysts wrote.

Blend ended the quarter with $44.2 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, and no debt.

#5574. TEN Holdings Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

(Nasdaq: XHLD), through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., the technology company behind TEN, a Digital Experience Platform that powers the next generation of enterprise digital engagement, today announced its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Third quarter revenue increased 17.9% year over year to $640,000, as we completed customer engagements that had been initiated in prior periods and added revenue from new customers," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings. "Our performance reflects continued demand for our digital engagement solutions and our ability to serve both existing and new customers. As we look ahead, our focus remains on expanding recurring revenue, strengthening our technology platform, and accelerating our transition toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model."

"Our third-quarter results reflect two significant expenses that we consider non-recurring: a $1.8 million write-off of previously capitalized service contracts and approximately $0.5 million in legal expenses. Excluding these items, our underlying selling, general and administrative expenses declined compared to the same period last year, reflecting the progress we have made in improving operational efficiency. Over the past 12 months, we have reduced our annual operating cost structure by approximately $2.5 million through strategic cost reductions, process improvements, and the integration of AI-driven tools to streamline engineering and accelerate product development. With these efficiencies largely implemented and a leaner operating structure in place, we are now shifting our focus toward accelerating revenue growth, expanding customer relationships, and scaling TEN, our new platform."

"We also made significant progress in strengthening our balance sheet, reducing short-term related-party borrowings from $4.6 million at the beginning of the year to approximately $0.1 million as of September 30, 2026. Total liabilities declined by approximately 74%, from $7.7 million at year-end 2025 to $2.0 million, reflecting our continued efforts to simplify our capital structure and improve our financial position."

"One of our most significant milestones this year was the launch of TEN, our next-generation Digital Experience Platform, whose development was accelerated by investments made possible through the proceeds of our June common stock offering, consistent with our previously communicated commitment to product development. TEN represents an important step in our evolution toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model, bringing together the tools organizations need to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences within a unified platform.

At launch, TEN provides enterprises with a self-service solution for webinars, virtual events, and continuing education programs, with the capacity to support up to 50,000 concurrent attendees. Building on our longstanding relationships with enterprise customers, many of whom rely on our technology for recurring digital engagement initiatives, we see a meaningful opportunity to transition these relationships toward subscription-based arrangements. We believe this approach will deliver greater flexibility and value to our customers while creating a more predictable and recurring revenue stream for TEN Holdings."

"Looking ahead, we are focused on three priorities: continuing the transition of our business from a managed services provider to a SaaS company, investing in TEN so that it remains competitive, and executing an acquisition strategy aimed at accretive businesses that add revenue and EBITDA, products our sales team can scale, and technology that complements our own. With TEN now in the market, a leaner cost structure, and a simplified balance sheet, we believe TEN Holdings is positioned to build a more scalable, recurring revenue business and create long-term value for our shareholders."
